interactions: Valproate + lamotrigine: valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations; while both are taken, start lamotrigine at half the usual dose and titrate at half the usual rate; the risk of serious rash is higher.

Ethinylestradiol + lamotrigine: estrogen roughly halves lamotrigine concentrations, which rise in the pill-free week; once valproate is withdrawn, lamotrigine falls and the dose usually needs to rise.
Ethinylestradiol + valproate: the combined pill can modestly lower valproate concentrations; valproate does not reduce contraceptive efficacy.
Levetiracetam: no interaction with valproate, clobazam or hormonal contraception.
Clobazam + valproate: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; additive sedation.

output.query: tuberous sclerosis complex focal epilepsy management in adults

results.finding: Adults with tuberous sclerosis complex need lifelong surveillance: abdominal MRI for angiomyolipoma every 1 to 3 years, renal function and blood pressure, chest CT screening for lymphangioleiomyomatosis in women from 18 years, dermatologic and dental review, ophthalmologic review when indicated, annual screening for TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders and ECG every 3 to 5 years.
results.source: Northrup H et al., Pediatr Neurol 2021;123:50-66 | Updated International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Diagnostic Criteria and Surveillance and Management Recommendations

results.finding: In treatment-resistant TSC-associated focal seizures, adjunctive everolimus gave a 50% responder rate of 28% (low exposure) and 40% (high exposure) against 15% with placebo.
results.source: French JA et al., Lancet 2016;388:2153-2163 | Adjunctive everolimus therapy for treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis (EXIST-3): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study

results.finding: Major congenital malformations were most frequent with valproate (about 10%, dose-dependent) and least frequent with lamotrigine and levetiracetam (about 3%).
results.source: Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:530-538 | Comparative risk of major congenital malformations with eight different antiepileptic drugs: a prospective cohort study of the EURAP registry

output.summary: TSC needs multisystem lifelong surveillance (Northrup 2021); everolimus is an adjunct for treatment-resistant TSC seizures (EXIST-3); valproate carries the highest malformation risk among antiseizure medicines (EURAP 2018).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not answer the breakthrough seizures by raising valproate as the long-term plan in a woman of childbearing potential.
Do not start carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin without changing contraception: they reduce combined pill efficacy.
Do not prescribe zonisamide: it is a sulfonamide and she has a sulfonamide allergy.
Do not attribute the episodes to panic attacks.
required_recommendations: Replace valproate with levetiracetam or lamotrigine as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, cross-titrating without abrupt withdrawal, chosen because valproate is teratogenic in a woman of childbearing potential (levetiracetam has no interaction with her pill; lamotrigine needs a halved titration while valproate continues).

Until valproate is stopped, keep her in the valproate pregnancy prevention programme with highly effective contraception (preferably an intrauterine device or implant, or the combined pill plus a barrier method).
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.
Address the missed doses as the provocation: adherence aids, a simple regimen and sleep regularity.

Arrange TSC surveillance per the 2021 international recommendations: abdominal MRI for angiomyolipoma, renal function and blood pressure, chest CT for lymphangioleiomyomatosis, dermatologic, dental and neuropsychiatric review.

Reserve adjunctive everolimus for TSC-associated seizures that become drug-resistant; refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation of the left mesial temporal tuber and hippocampal sclerosis if seizures continue despite two appropriate ASMs.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Advise on safety while she lives alone and works in a laboratory (showers rather than baths, no unsupervised hazardous laboratory work until seizures are controlled).
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, back to baseline and a clear provocation (missed doses) in known epilepsy: no indication for lumbar puncture.
Aura, automatisms and a convulsion with tongue bite are epileptic; the stable childhood rhabdomyoma is asymptomatic and raises no syncope question.
Back to baseline, no head injury or anticoagulation, MRI available: CT cannot show the tuber or the hippocampal sclerosis.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin secondary to tuberous sclerosis complex (mesial-temporal cortical tuber and ipsilateral hippocampal sclerosis — dual pathology)

differential.diagnosis: Multifocal epilepsy of TSC with an extratemporal (right frontal) focus
differential.key_features: The right frontal tuber could be epileptogenic, but the epigastric aura, oral and manual automatisms, postictal word-finding difficulty and the left temporal EEG abnormality point to the left mesial temporal lesions.

differential.diagnosis: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type II without TSC
differential.key_features: Multiple hypomelanotic macules, a fibrous cephalic plaque, a cardiac rhabdomyoma, a subependymal nodule and more than one tuber establish TSC clinically.
MRI shows only a small calcified non-enhancing subependymal nodule without hydrocephalus.
Her own attribution; stereotyped epigastric aura with impaired awareness, automatisms, postictal confusion and progression to a convulsion are epileptic.
Stereotyped temporal semiology, a convulsion with lateral tongue bite, a low valproate level and a concordant EEG and MRI.
An epigastric aura with automatisms and 15-30 minutes of confusion are not syncope.

key_clinical_evidence: Epigastric rising aura, impaired awareness with lip-smacking and manual automatisms, postictal confusion and a first convulsion are recurrent focal seizures of mesial temporal type after 15 seizure-free years.
MRI shows a left mesial temporal tuber and separate left hippocampal sclerosis (dual pathology) with other TSC lesions; the EEG abnormality is left anterior temporal, concordant.
Valproic acid 38 mcg/mL after admitted missed doses: non-adherence is the provocation of the breakthrough.

Valproate in a 29-year-old woman needs a pregnancy prevention programme and a planned switch; valproate doubles and ethinylestradiol halves lamotrigine, and zonisamide is excluded by the sulfonamide allergy.
TSC is a multisystem disease: renal, pulmonary, dermatologic and neuropsychiatric surveillance continues regardless of seizure control.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old right-handed woman with a known history of tuberous sclerosis complex and remote infantile spasms presents to the neurology service after being admitted through the emergency department following a witnessed generalized convulsion at her university laboratory. She reports a 3-month history of recurrent stereotyped episodes beginning with an indescribable 'rising sensation' in her stomach followed by an altered sense of awareness during which she appears to stare blankly and perform repetitive lip-smacking and fumbling movements with her right hand. These episodes last approximately 60 to 90 seconds, after which she experiences confusion and mild headache lasting 15 to 30 minutes. She initially attributed the episodes to anxiety and panic attacks, especially given the stress of her graduate studies. Over the past three weeks, the frequency has increased from once weekly to nearly daily, and yesterday's episode progressed to bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions witnessed by her laboratory supervisor, who called emergency services. She was found to be confused and somnolent on arrival, with a tongue bite on the left lateral margin. She denies any recent illness, fever, or new medications. She takes valproic acid and clobazam but acknowledges missing doses several times over the past month because of her schedule. She had been seizure-free since age 14 and had considered discontinuing her antiepileptic medications with her previous neurologist two years ago but ultimately decided to continue them. She reports no recent head trauma, no changes in sleep pattern beyond occasionally staying late in the lab, and no exposure to flashing lights or other known seizure triggers.

neurological_exam.additional: Dermatologic examination notable for three hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf spots) on the upper back and one on the left anterior thigh, each approximately 2-4 cm. Small fibrous plaque on the forehead consistent with fibrous cephalic plaque. No facial angiofibromas.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation and motor function symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady, narrow-based gait. Tandem walk intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Speech fluent with intact naming and repetition. Able to recall 2/3 objects at 5 minutes. Mild word-finding difficulty noted during spontaneous conversation, though formal confrontation naming was intact. Affect mildly anxious but appropriate.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all four extremities proximally and distally. No drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
